questions.answer: Lists are ordered, mutable, allow mixed types and duplicates. Index 0-based + negative; slice [start:stop:step] excludes stop. `l[0]='x'` works because mutable, unlike strings/tuples.
questions.question: What defines a list and how do indexing/slicing work?

questions.answer: append(x) adds one item (list becomes nested); extend(iter) adds each element flat; insert(i,x) at position. remove(v) first value (ValueError if missing); pop()/pop(i) by index and returns it.
questions.question: Compare append vs extend vs insert and remove vs pop.

questions.answer: sort()/reverse() mutate in place, return None; sorted()/slicing [::-1] make new. copy() is shallow (nested shared, need deepcopy); `b=a` aliases same object.
questions.question: Which list ops mutate vs create new? Explain copy/aliasing.

questions.answer: Because sort() mutates and returns None; r=None. Fix: `nums.sort(); result=nums` or `result=sorted(nums)`. Same for reverse(). Also append([3,4]) nests — use extend for flat.
questions.question: Trap: `r = nums.sort(); print(r)` is None and `a.append([3,4])` nests. Explain.

questions.answer: `b=a` aliases — both point to same list so append affects a; use `b=a.copy()`. But copy() is shallow: nested `m[0].append(99)` still affects original; use deepcopy for nested.
